content: Post-extraction bleeding (PEB) is a well-recognized and frequently encountered complication in dental practice. It is defined as bleeding that persists beyond 8 to 12 hours after a dental extraction. The reported incidence of PEB varies widely, ranging from 0% to 26%. If left untreated, PEB can lead to complications that range from localized soft tissue hematomas to significant blood loss. The causes of PEB can be categorized as either local or systemic. Local causes include bleeding from soft tissues or bone at the extraction site. Systemic causes may involve platelet dysfunction, coagulation disorders, excessive fibrinolysis, or inherited and acquired conditions, such as those induced by medications. A variety of techniques have been proposed to manage PEB, targeting both local and systemic factors contributing to the bleeding. This document is an update of a review originally published in June 2016. The objective of the review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions for managing different types of PEB. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including Cochrane Oral Health’s Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL. The search also included the US National Institutes of Health Trials Registry (ClinicalTrials.gov) and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing trials. Additionally, reference lists of relevant systematic reviews were examined. The review considered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed any intervention for treating PEB. Participants of any age, gender, and type of tooth (anterior or posterior, mandibular or maxillary) were included. The trials could compare one intervention with another, with a placebo, or with no treatment at all. Three pairs of review authors independently screened the search results. Full-text articles were obtained for potentially relevant trials. If data had been extracted, the statistical analysis would have followed the methods outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. However, the review did not identify any randomized controlled trials that met the inclusion criteria. As a result, no reliable evidence was found to evaluate the effects of different interventions for treating PEB. In the absence of robust evidence, clinicians must rely on their clinical expertise and judgment to determine the most appropriate treatment for PEB, taking into account individual patient factors. There is a clear need for well-designed and rigorously conducted clinical trials on this topic. Future studies should adhere to the CONSORT guidelines to ensure high-quality reporting and methodology.
